conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. We’re going to spend a few minutes with a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past week so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything we discuss is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no “right” or “wrong” answer, only what’s true for you. I’ll ask 10 questions, one at a time, and we’ll go at your pace.

Whenever you’re ready, we can start.  
First, how often in the past seven days have you found yourself feeling low or miserable, even when things around you were going okay?

I’ve felt that way a few times this week—maybe three or four days. Nothing major went wrong, but I’d just get this heavy feeling out of nowhere, like a cloud sitting on me. It usually passes if I keep busy with the baby, but it keeps popping back up.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—just not as easily as before. My partner or my mom will say something silly and I’ll chuckle, but it feels kind of forced. I’d say I’ve genuinely laughed maybe once or twice in the past week, and even then it fades pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Some days I do—like when my sister said she’d bring coffee yesterday morning, I actually felt a little spark of “that’ll be nice.” But most of the time it’s kind of flat. I’ll think, “Oh, that could be fun,” yet the excitement doesn’t really kick in the way it used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times. Yesterday the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I’m not soothing him the right way. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but I still caught myself going, “If I were better at this, he wouldn’t be so upset.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little—mostly at night when the house is quiet. I’ll lie down and suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing is too faint or that I missed a dirty diaper and he’ll get a rash. I can usually tell myself it’s silly and calm back down, but it still pops up out of nowhere maybe every other day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick flutter of “what if something bad happens?” It’s more like a brief wave of nerves than a real scare, and it’s gone in a minute or two.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can check things off. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the pile of laundry or the dishes, and it’s like a little weight on my chest. I usually manage to push through, but it’s been harder than before to feel on top of it all.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really—once I finally get to bed I drift off okay. It’s just that sometimes I lie there thinking about everything I didn’t finish or worrying I’ll sleep through the baby’s cry, so it takes me an extra twenty minutes or so to settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, I’ve had that feeling most days this week. It’s not constant, but it shows up in little waves—like I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly feel like I’m about to tear up for no real reason. I’d say four, maybe five days out of the past seven.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice. Once was when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him; the other time was after a phone call with my mom—she meant well, but I just got overwhelmed and the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that over the past week you've felt low most days, with joy seeming distant and laughter feeling forced. You described waves of <sym>sadness</sym> and occasional tears, alongside worries about your baby's safety that pop up at night, yet you've still managed to push through daily tasks while feeling overwhelmed. Your honesty about these <sym>emotional struggles</sym> while caring for your newborn highlights how common yet tough the postpartum period can be, and your wellbeing matters.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response indicates marked reduction in ability to laugh naturally, with laughter feeling forced and infrequent over past week.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only occasional, muted enjoyment that "doesn't really kick in," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a couple of times" with specific examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, unprovoked worries several times per week that intrude at quiet moments, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most days" (4–5/7), but not "most of the time" each day; semantic fit is "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the 13+ cutoff indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse <sym>low mood</sym> most days, <sym>anhedonia</sym> described as "flat" or "spark fades fast," <sym>self-criticism</sym> about parenting, frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> focused on infant safety, and multiple crying episodes. These features align with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood, diminished interest, guilt, and clinically significant distress. No self-harm ideation is present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation
2. Share these screening results with your obstetrician or midwife at your next visit
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks and benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track symptom change
5. Enlist practical help from family or friends for household tasks and baby care to reduce overwhelm
6. Practice daily 10-15 minute self-care breaks: gentle walking outdoors, brief mindfulness, or a warm shower
7. Maintain consistent sleep routine; nap when baby naps and limit screen time before bed
8. Join a local or online new-mothers support group to share experiences and reduce isolation
9. Store emergency numbers in your phone: your provider's office, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and a trusted friend for immediate support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days this week  
- Markedly reduced enjoyment/interest (“flat,” “spark fades fast”)  
- Self-blame regarding infant care (“I must be doing something wrong”)  
- Recurrent, unprovoked worries about infant safety, middle-of-the-night rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, “little weight on chest”  
- Mild sleep-onset delay related to racing thoughts  
- No anhedonia absolutely, but pleasure markedly blunted; laughter described as forced  

Pattern: Symptoms present ≥4–5 days/week, causing subjective distress but no impairment in basic functioning; no self-harm ideation.

Potential screening significance:  
• Score range and endorsement pattern consistent with mild-to-moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; does not meet threshold for panic or suicidal risk at this time.

Risk factors noted:  
- Daily sadness and crying spells  
- Guilt/cognitive self-criticism  
- Anxiety focused on infant well-being  
- Sleep disruption secondary to worry

Safety: Denies thoughts of self-harm; no protective concerns identified.

Overall screening impression:  
Positive findings for mood and anxiety symptoms post-delivery; further evaluation with standardized tool (EPDS) and clinical interview recommended to clarify severity and guide support / treatment planning.
